enonce_intro_markdown:
The marks obtained by 10 students in Mathematics and Physics in an end of year examination are shown in the table below.

| Mathematics, $x$ | 60 | 22 | 7 | 13 | 41 | 33 | 31 | 30 | 40 | 26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Physics, $y$ | 48 | 11 | 2 | 3 | 27 | 26 | 20 | 19 | 32 | 14 |

If required, you may use $\left(\sum x = 303,\ \sum x^2 = 11209,\ \sum y = 202,\ \sum y^2 = 5824,\ \sum xy = 7974\right)$.
incertitudes: Question 8 : les sommes imprimées dans le sujet ($\sum x = 303$, $\sum x^2 = 11209$, $\sum y = 202$, $\sum y^2 = 5824$, $\sum xy = 7974$) ont été recalculées à partir du tableau par script : elles sont exactes. Les points imprimés par partie, 8, 2, 2 et 1, totalisent 13 ; recopiés tels quels.

Question 8 (b) : la droite est donnée sous la forme $y = a + bx$ avec $a = -7.49$ et $b = 0.914$ (valeurs plus précises : $a = -7.48997$, $b = 0.913860$) ; en (c) l'estimation est 15.36 avec les coefficients arrondis (15.357 avec les coefficients exacts), soit environ 15 points.

questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Calculate, correct to four decimal places, the Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient of Mathematics and Physics.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Pearson's coefficient is $r = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}\,S_{yy}}}$ with $n = 10$ and

$$S_{xx} = \sum x^2 - \frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}, \quad S_{yy} = \sum y^2 - \frac{(\sum y)^2}{n}, \quad S_{xy} = \sum xy - \frac{\sum x \sum y}{n}.$$

$$S_{xx} = 11209 - \frac{303^2}{10} = 11209 - 9180.9 = 2028.1$$

$$S_{yy} = 5824 - \frac{202^2}{10} = 5824 - 4080.4 = 1743.6$$

$$S_{xy} = 7974 - \frac{303 \times 202}{10} = 7974 - 6120.6 = 1853.4$$

$$r = \frac{1853.4}{\sqrt{2028.1 \times 1743.6}} = \frac{1853.4}{\sqrt{3536195.2}} = \frac{1853.4}{1880.48} = 0.9856$$

**$r = 0.9856$** (to 4 decimal places): a very strong positive linear correlation between the Mathematics and Physics marks.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Determine the equation of the least squares regression line of Physics marks on Mathematics marks.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = a + bx$ with $b = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.

$$b = \frac{1853.4}{2028.1} = 0.9139$$

$$\bar{x} = \frac{303}{10} = 30.3, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{202}{10} = 20.2$$

$$a = 20.2 - 0.91386 \times 30.3 = 20.2 - 27.69 = -7.49$$

**The regression line of Physics marks ($y$) on Mathematics marks ($x$) is $y = -7.49 + 0.914x$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Estimate the Physics marks of a student who scored $25$ marks in Mathematics.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Substitute $x = 25$ into the regression line:

$$y = -7.49 + 0.914 \times 25 = -7.49 + 22.85 = 15.36$$

**The estimated Physics mark is about $15$** ($15.4$ to 1 decimal place).

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Give a reason why, you cannot use your line to estimate the Physics marks of a student who scored $65$ marks in Mathematics.
questions.corrige_markdown: The Mathematics marks in the data range from $7$ to $60$. A mark of $65$ lies **outside this range**, so using the line would be **extrapolation**: the linear relationship observed between $7$ and $60$ is not known to continue beyond $60$, and the estimate (about $52$) would be unreliable.
